newsitem.title: INDIA: FUND VIEW-India bond issues seen offering safe bet.
newsitem.headline: FUND VIEW-India bond issues seen offering safe bet.

text.p: Indian mutual funds are lining up to launch fixed-income schemes in an attempt to lure investors away from the country's volatile stock markets to dormant but "safe" debt markets, analysts said on Wednesday.

"January has not exactly been the best advertisement for equities," said Ajay Srinivasan, chief investment officer at ITC Threadneedle, a joint venture between India's ITC Classic Finance and Threadneedle Asset Management Limited of the U.K.
The firm is likely to launch a debt fund in March.
"The (stock) market has been so volatile that people are willing to go for debt," Srinivasan said.

Indian shares have fluctuated wildly since the start of the year. Prices rose sharply in January on government assurances that a new package of market-boosting reforms would be unveiled. But hopes were dashed last week when the government said the expected package actually consisted of measures already taken since January, prompting a steep sell-off in stocks.
Analysts say share prices will remain volatile in the run-up to India's federal budget, due on February 28.
Leading players which are preparing to launch debt funds in the coming months include Tata Asset Management, Alliance Capital, ITC Threadneedle, Birla Capital, Sundaram Newton and Merrill Lynch.
"It's not just a fad," said the country manager of a company preparing to launch its debt fund later this month.
"Investor interest in debt can be seen in the success rate of bond issues since last year," he said.
Indian equities were in the doldrums for most of last year and firms turned to the debt market, raising more than 60 billion rupees through a series of successful bond issues.
The secondary market for debt instruments is in its infancy with little activity. Debt trades are currently limited to government securities, or gilts.
"For the mutual fund industry, it has become easier to do a debt product today than it was under the old regulations," the country manager said.
"There was pent up supply in the pipeline and you're seeing some of that supply manifest itself," he said.
The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI), the market regulator, recently eased rules for debt market mutual funds.
SEBI said it had cleared 14 schemes which plan to invest primarily in the debt market after the rules were relaxed.
U.S. investment company Templeton fired the debt-fund trend by launching its domestic income fund earlier this week.
"We have growing confidence in the structure of the bond market," Douglas Lempereur, director for corporate development at Templeton Investment Counsel, Inc, said at the launch.
"Today we see the elements of a more mature bond market," Lempereur said, citing recent moves to boost liquidity in the debt market, including allowing foreigners to invest in gilts.
Sundaram Newton, a partnership between south India's Sundaram Finance and the U.K.'s Newton Investment Management Ltd, plans an equity scheme in February and a debt scheme in March.
The advertisement for its schemes emphasises safety.
"Sundaram Mutual Fund believes that wealth can't be made overnight," it says.
"In 1994, a flood of equity-oriented schemes took a bad beating and investors are now looking for assured returns," said R. Ramesh, Sundaram Newton's chief marketing officer.
Many equity-linked mutual funds -- which were launched in 1994 when Bombay's benchmark index hit its all-time high -- have performed miserably in the last coupleof years.
